M7.Hebb.Title: Synaptic plasticity: Hebb, Oja and PCA
M7.Hebb.Lead: Learning in the nervous system mostly means that existing connections change. With synaptic plasticity the same presynaptic activity later causes a larger or smaller postsynaptic effect. A simple local rule – strengthen connections whose two sides are active together – already makes a neuron learn the statistical structure of its input: its principal component.
M7.Hebb.C1.Title: LTP and LTD
M7.Hebb.C1.Text: Long-term potentiation (LTP) is a lasting increase, long-term depression (LTD) a lasting decrease of synaptic efficacy – lasting minutes, hours, days or longer. In models both are a change of the weight w. The best-known mechanism is the NMDA receptor: when glutamate release coincides with postsynaptic depolarization, Ca²⁺ enters, and the calcium signal changes AMPA-receptor number and spine structure. A large, fast Ca²⁺ signal tends to give LTP, a weaker one LTD.
M7.Hebb.C2.Title: Hebb's rule and why it is unstable
M7.Hebb.C2.Text: “Neurons that fire together wire together”: τ_w dw/dt = u v with v = w·u. The rule is local – each synapse needs only its own input u_i and the output v – which makes it biologically plausible. But larger w gives larger v, which makes w grow even faster: positive feedback. Without normalization the weight vector grows without bound: d‖w‖²/dt = 2v²/τ_w > 0.
M7.Hebb.C3.Title: Covariance rule and Oja's rule
M7.Hebb.C3.Text: The covariance rule compares the output with its mean, u(v − ⟨v⟩): above-average responses strengthen, below-average ones weaken a synapse, so LTP and LTD appear in one rule – but it is still unstable. Oja's rule adds a decay term that grows with v²: τ_w dw/dt = u v − α v² w. The norm of w settles at 1/√α while its direction keeps turning towards the dominant structure of the input.
M7.Hebb.C4.Title: The neuron learns the principal component
M7.Hebb.C4.Text: Averaged over inputs, Hebbian learning becomes τ_w dw/dt = Q w, with Q the input correlation (or C the covariance) matrix. Written in Q's eigenvectors, each component grows as exp(λ_i t/τ_w): the one with the largest eigenvalue wins. With normalization (Oja), w aligns with the principal eigenvector – the first principal component, the direction of maximal variance. But PCA finds directions of variance, not clusters: for two separate blobs it just points along the long axis joining them.
M7.Hebb.Formulas:
v = w · u = wᵀu | Output of a linear neuron.
τ_w dw/dt = u v | Hebb's rule (unstable).
τ_w dw/dt = u (v − ⟨v⟩)   ⟹   τ_w dw/dt = C w | Covariance rule: LTP and LTD; the averaged dynamics follow the covariance matrix C.
τ_w dw/dt = u v − α v² w | Oja's rule: ‖w‖ → 1/√α, w → principal eigenvector.
Q e_i = λ_i e_i,   w(t) = Σ_i c_i(0) exp(λ_i t/τ_w) e_i | The component with the largest eigenvalue dominates.
M7.Hebb.Bio: Real neurons use several stabilizing mechanisms at once – homeostatic plasticity, synaptic scaling, limited receptor trafficking, adaptation of inhibition and metaplasticity – which keep Hebbian positive feedback from running away. The timing-dependent version of Hebb's rule, STDP, is explored in the STDP lab: pre-before-post gives LTP, post-before-pre LTD.
M7.Hebb.ML: PCA is linear dimensionality reduction: if most of the variance lies along a few directions, the data can be represented with fewer coordinates. Oja's neuron is an online, local, “neural” PCA algorithm; Sanger's rule extends it to several components.
M7.Hebb.Takeaways:
LTP is a lasting strengthening, LTD a lasting weakening of a synapse.
Hebb: Δw ∝ u·v – co-active pre- and postsynaptic units strengthen their connection.
The plain Hebb and covariance rules are unstable without normalization.
Oja's rule keeps ‖w‖ finite and learns the principal-component direction.
PCA looks for directions of variance; it does not discover clusters.
M7.Hebb.Q1: What is the difference between LTP and LTD?
M7.Hebb.A1: LTP is a lasting increase, LTD a lasting decrease of the postsynaptic effect of the same presynaptic input.
M7.Hebb.Q2: How is the simplest Hebb rule written, and why is it a local learning rule?
M7.Hebb.A2: τ_w dw/dt = u v; updating one weight needs only its own presynaptic activity and the postsynaptic activity.
M7.Hebb.Q3: Why is the pure Hebb rule unstable?
M7.Hebb.A3: Larger w gives larger v, which makes w grow even faster – without normalization the weights run away.
M7.Hebb.Q4: What does the normalizing term of Oja's rule do?
M7.Hebb.A4: It is a negative, activity-dependent term (−α v² w) that limits the growth of the weight norm.
M7.Hebb.Q5: Why do eigenvectors of the correlation/covariance matrix appear in Hebbian learning?
M7.Hebb.A5: Because the averaged dynamics are τ_w dw/dt = Q w (or C w); in the eigenvector basis each component grows independently according to its eigenvalue, and the largest one wins.
M7.Hebb.Guide:
Pick “Hebb (unstable)”: w turns towards the cloud's axis but its length explodes – look at the ‖w‖ plot.
Pick “Oja”: the arrow settles on the dashed principal axis with length 1/√α.
Pick “Shifted cloud (Oja)”: Oja finds the correlation axis through the origin, not the cloud's own axis.
“Covariance rule” subtracts the mean and finds the true axis of variation – but its norm grows again.
“Two clusters”: PCA only finds the long axis joining the clusters, not the clusters themselves.
M7.Hebb.SimpleTitle: In plain words: the path that most people walk on
M7.Hebb.Simple: Imagine a lawn where people cross in all directions, but most of them walk roughly the same diagonal. Every footstep flattens the grass a little where it lands. After a while a path appears along the most popular direction. The arrow w is that path: every input that agrees with it makes it a bit stronger. Pure Hebb would keep digging the path deeper forever; Oja's rule also lets grass grow back, so the path keeps a fixed depth while still pointing in the main direction.
M7.Hebb.Rule.Tip: Hebb: Δw ∝ u v. Covariance: Δw ∝ (u − ⟨u⟩)(v − ⟨v⟩). Oja: Δw ∝ u v − α v² w.
M7.Hebb.Epsilon.Tip: Size of one weight update (ε = 1/τ_w in discrete time).
M7.Hebb.Alpha.Tip: Strength of Oja's normalizing term; the weight norm settles at 1/√α.
M7.Hebb.Reset.Tip: Restart from a new random small weight vector.
M7.Hebb.Data.Tip: 400 samples of a two-dimensional Gaussian cloud – the inputs u = (u₁, u₂) of the neuron.
M7.Hebb.Offset.Tip: Moves the cloud away from the origin, perpendicular to its axis. Then the correlation matrix (Hebb, Oja) and the covariance matrix point in different directions.
M7.Hebb.TwoClusters.Tip: Replaces the cloud by two tight blobs – a case where PCA misses the structure.
M7.Hebb.Plane.Tip: Violet dots: inputs. Teal arrow: the weight vector w (length capped on screen). Green dashed: principal eigenvector of the averaged matrix. Dotted circle: radius 1/√α. Yellow: the input just presented.
M7.Hebb.NormPlot.Tip: ‖w‖ over learning steps. Hebb and covariance: grows without bound (capped at 1000). Oja: settles at 1/√α.
M7.Hebb.AnglePlot.Tip: Angle between w and the principal eigenvector (0° = perfectly aligned).
M7.Hebb.Readout: steps {0}   ‖w‖ = {1}   angle to PC1 = {2}°   λ₁ = {3}, λ₂ = {4}
M7.Hebb.Explain.Hebb: Pure Hebb: the direction of w approaches the principal axis, but its length keeps growing (now {0}) – positive feedback without a brake.
M7.Hebb.Explain.Covariance: Covariance rule: inputs are measured relative to their mean, so w finds the true axis of variation of the shifted cloud – but ‖w‖ = {0} still grows without bound.
M7.Hebb.Explain.Oja: Oja's rule: ‖w‖ is pulled towards 1/√α = {0}, while the direction aligns with the principal eigenvector (now {1}° away). A local learning rule performs PCA.
M7.Hebb.Explain.Clusters: Two clusters: w points along the long axis joining the blobs – the direction of maximal variance – but nothing in the neuron represents the two groups separately. Clustering needs another mechanism (next lesson).
M7.Competitive.Title: Unsupervised learning: competition and clustering
M7.Competitive.Lead: In unsupervised learning the system receives inputs but no labels or desired outputs. It has to discover the statistical structure itself: clusters, low-dimensional structure, local features. A first neural answer: let output neurons compete, and turn each weight vector into the prototype of one group of inputs.
M7.Competitive.C1.Title: Neurons as prototypes
M7.Competitive.C1.Text: Each output neuron i has a weight vector w_i and responds with v_i = w_i·u. If the weight vectors sit at the centres of the data groups, each neuron represents one prototype, and a new input belongs to the neuron whose weights are most similar to it.
M7.Competitive.C2.Title: Why is the most active neuron the nearest one?
M7.Competitive.C2.Text: ‖u − w_i‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖w_i‖² − 2uᵀw_i. If all weight vectors have the same norm, the first two terms are the same for every neuron, so the smallest distance belongs to the neuron with the largest uᵀw_i – the most active one. Neural activity can therefore implement a nearest-prototype decision.
M7.Competitive.C3.Title: Winner-takes-all learning and K-means
M7.Competitive.C3.Text: For each input the output neurons compete; only the winner learns: Δw_i* = ε(u − w_i*). Geometrically the winning prototype takes a small step towards the input, and after many samples it sits at the mean of the inputs it wins – an online clustering algorithm. K-means does the same in batch form: assign every point to the nearest centroid, then move every centroid to the mean of its points.
M7.Competitive.C4.Title: Self-organizing maps
M7.Competitive.C4.Text: A self-organizing (Kohonen) map also updates the neighbours of the winner in the network: Δw_i = ε h(i, i*)(u − w_i). The neighbourhood kernel h starts wide and narrows during learning – first a global ordering, then local refinement. Neighbouring neurons come to represent neighbouring inputs: the map preserves topology, like the orientation maps of V1.
M7.Competitive.Formulas:
v_i = w_i · u | Output neuron i: activity = similarity to its prototype.
‖u − w_i‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖w_i‖² − 2 uᵀw_i | With equal norms the most active neuron is the nearest.
i* = argmin_i ‖u − w_i‖²,    Δw_i* = ε (u − w_i*) | Winner-takes-all competitive learning.
c_n = argmin_k ‖u_n − μ_k‖²,   μ_k = mean{u_n : c_n = k} | K-means: assignment step and centroid update.
Δw_i = ε · h(i, i*) · (u − w_i) | Self-organizing map: the winner's neighbours learn too.
M7.Competitive.Bio: Lateral inhibition between cortical neurons can implement soft winner-takes-all competition. Topographic maps – somatotopy, tonotopy, orientation and ocular-dominance maps in V1 – are often modelled as self-organizing maps shaped by input statistics during development.
M7.Competitive.ML: Competitive learning is an online, neural cousin of K-means: winner selection is the assignment step, the prototype update the centroid step. SOMs are used for visualizing high-dimensional data on a 2-D grid.
M7.Competitive.Takeaways:
PCA looks for directions of variance; clustering looks for prototypes of natural groups.
With equal norms the most active output neuron is the one whose weights are closest to the input.
Competitive learning moves only the winner towards the input – closely related to K-means.
In a SOM the winner's neighbours learn too, so a topology-preserving map forms.
M7.Competitive.Q1: What is the difference between the goals of PCA and of clustering?
M7.Competitive.A1: PCA looks for directions of maximal variance; clustering looks for prototypes of natural groups of data.
M7.Competitive.Q2: How does winner-takes-all competitive learning work?
M7.Competitive.A2: The most active (nearest) prototype wins, and only its weights move a small step towards the input.
M7.Competitive.Q3: What is the relation between competitive learning and K-means?
M7.Competitive.A3: Choosing the winner corresponds to the assignment step; moving the prototype towards the mean is the online version of the centroid update.
M7.Competitive.Q4: What does a self-organizing map add to plain competitive learning?
M7.Competitive.A4: It also updates the winner's neighbours, so the neural map preserves part of the topology of the input space.
M7.Competitive.Guide:
With “WTA” and three blobs, press Run: the prototypes leave the centre and settle in the blobs.
Set the number of neurons to 2 for three blobs – one prototype has to sit between two groups.
Switch to K-means: every iteration jumps all centroids to their cluster means at once.
Choose SOM with the “Ring” data: the chain of neurons unfolds and lines up along the ring.
Click into the plane to add a new cluster and watch the network adapt.
M7.Competitive.SimpleTitle: In plain words: ice-cream stands on a beach
M7.Competitive.Simple: Imagine a few ice-cream sellers on a beach where people sit in groups. Every customer walks to the nearest stand, and after each sale the seller moves a tiny step towards that customer. After a while every seller stands in the middle of one group of people – without anyone telling them where the groups are. That is competitive learning. In a self-organizing map the sellers are also tied together with a rope, so neighbouring sellers end up serving neighbouring groups.
M7.Competitive.Algorithm.Tip: WTA: online winner-takes-all. K-means: batch assignment + mean. SOM: Kohonen map, a chain of neurons with shrinking neighbourhood.
M7.Competitive.Explain.Competitive: Each input is presented to all neurons; the nearest (most active) one wins and moves a step ε towards it. The coloured cells show which input region each neuron wins.
M7.Competitive.Explain.KMeans: Each iteration assigns every point to the nearest centroid, then moves every centroid to the mean of its points. The distortion can only decrease.
M7.Competitive.Explain.SelfOrganizingMap: The neurons form a chain (white line). The winner and its chain-neighbours move towards the input; the neighbourhood shrinks over time, so the chain first unfolds globally, then refines locally.
M7.Competitive.Count.Tip: Number of prototypes (K). For the SOM try 10–20.
M7.Competitive.Regions: Show regions won by each neuron
M7.Competitive.Regions.Tip: Colours the plane by the nearest prototype (Voronoi cells) – the decision boundaries of the nearest-prototype rule.
M7.Competitive.Data.Tip: Unlabelled 2-D inputs. The network never sees colours or labels – the colours show its own assignment.
M7.Competitive.ClickHint: Click in the plane to drop a new cluster of 25 points.
M7.Competitive.Plane.Tip: Dots: inputs coloured by their winning neuron. Big glowing dots: prototypes w_k with their recent trail. White dashed: last input and its winner.
M7.Competitive.Distortion.Tip: Mean squared distance of the points to their prototype – what K-means minimizes.
M7.Em.Title: Generative models: Gaussian mixtures and EM
M7.Em.Lead: A deeper question than clustering: which hidden process could have generated the data? A generative model first draws a hidden cause from a prior, then generates the observation from the likelihood. Learning means finding parameters that explain the data; perception means inferring the hidden causes – the posterior.
M7.Em.C1.Title: Prior, likelihood, posterior
M7.Em.C1.Text: The prior p(v) says what is probable before seeing data. The likelihood p(u|v) says how probable an observation is if we know its hidden cause. The posterior p(v|u) is the result of inference: how probable each cause is after seeing the data. Bayes' rule connects them. The prior is not a prejudice in the everyday sense, but the model's probabilistic structure before the data.
M7.Em.C2.Title: Gaussian mixture: soft assignment
M7.Em.C2.Text: In a Gaussian mixture model every cluster k is a Gaussian with mean μ_k, covariance Σ_k and mixing weight π_k. Competitive learning makes hard assignments – one input, one winner. The posterior of a mixture gives soft assignments, for example 0.8 for cluster A and 0.2 for B, which matters for overlapping, uncertain clusters.
M7.Em.C3.Title: Expectation–Maximization
M7.Em.C3.Text: We would need the parameters to know who belongs where, and the assignments to estimate the parameters. EM breaks the circle by alternating: E-step – compute every point's posterior responsibility r_nk = p(k|u_n) with the current parameters; M-step – re-estimate π, μ and Σ from the responsibility-weighted points. Each iteration can only increase the likelihood. K-means is its “hard” relative with 0/1 responsibilities and round clusters.
M7.Em.C4.Title: What are the hidden causes of natural images?
M7.Em.C4.Text: For point clouds the hidden cause is a cluster label. Natural images contain thousands of pixels shaped by edges, textures, surfaces, objects, lighting and viewpoint. The next lesson asks which hidden causes explain local image structure – not just global directions of variance.
M7.Em.Formulas:
v ~ p(v; G),   u ~ p(u | v; G) | Generative model: hidden cause from the prior, observation from the likelihood.
p(u; G) = Σ_v p(u | v; G) p(v; G) | Marginal probability of the data.
p(v | u) = p(u | v) p(v) / p(u) | Bayes' rule: the posterior.
p(u) = Σ_k π_k · N(u; μ_k, Σ_k) | Gaussian mixture model.
E: r_nk = p(k | u_n)    M: μ_k = Σ_n r_nk u_n / Σ_n r_nk, … | The two alternating steps of EM.
M7.Em.Bio: The Bayesian-brain hypothesis proposes that perception is inference: the brain combines prior expectations with noisy sensory likelihoods. Many psychophysical experiments (cue combination, visual illusions) are explained well by near-optimal Bayesian inference.
M7.Em.ML: Gaussian mixtures and EM are classic tools of unsupervised learning; latent-variable models such as factor analysis, variational autoencoders and diffusion models share the same structure: a prior over latent causes, a likelihood that generates the data, and approximate posterior inference.
M7.Em.Takeaways:
Generative model: prior + likelihood; inference: the posterior via Bayes' rule.
A Gaussian mixture is a probabilistic cluster model with means, covariances and mixing weights.
EM alternates posterior responsibilities (E) and parameter re-estimation (M).
Hard assignment (K-means) vs soft assignment (GMM posterior).
M7.Em.Q1: What do prior, likelihood and posterior mean?
M7.Em.A1: Prior: distribution of hidden causes before the data; likelihood: p(u|v); posterior: p(v|u), the probability of the causes after observing u.
M7.Em.Q2: What is the difference between hard and soft cluster assignment?
M7.Em.A2: Hard assignment picks a single cluster (0/1); soft assignment gives posterior probabilities for several clusters.
M7.Em.Q3: What happens in the E-step and in the M-step of EM?
M7.Em.A3: E-step: posterior responsibilities of the components for every point; M-step: re-estimation of the parameters weighted by them.
M7.Em.Q4: Why is K-means a “hard” relative of EM?
M7.Em.A4: Its responsibilities are 0 or 1 and it assumes equal, round clusters, minimizing distances instead of maximizing a likelihood.
M7.Em.Guide:
Press “Half step” repeatedly: after an E-step the point colours change (soft assignment), after an M-step the ellipses move.
Run EM and watch the log-likelihood rise and level off.
Move the mouse over the plane: the Bayes panel shows prior, likelihood and posterior for that point.
Points between the blobs get mixed colours – they are genuinely uncertain.
Press “Dream samples”: the model generates new data from its prior and likelihood.
M7.Em.SimpleTitle: In plain words: guessing which bag a marble came from
M7.Em.Simple: Imagine marbles drawn from a few hidden bags, each bag making marbles of a typical colour and size. You only see the marbles. EM is a two-step guessing game: first, for every marble you guess how likely it came from each bag (E-step); then you redescribe each bag from the marbles that probably came from it (M-step). Repeating these two steps, your picture of the bags gets better and better. A marble halfway between two bags really is uncertain – that is why it gets a mixed colour.
M7.Em.Algorithm.Tip: Fits a Gaussian mixture model to the unlabelled points.
M7.Em.Count.Tip: Number of Gaussian components (hidden causes) in the model.
M7.Em.HalfStep.Tip: Performs only the next E-step or M-step, so the two phases can be seen separately.
M7.Em.Phase.AfterE: E-step done: responsibilities updated (point colours). Next: M-step.
M7.Em.Phase.AfterM: M-step done: means, covariances and weights updated (ellipses). Next: E-step.
M7.Em.Generate.Tip: Draws new samples from the fitted model: first a component k from the prior π, then a point from N(μ_k, Σ_k).
M7.Em.Generate.Text: A generative model can do more than label data – it can “dream” new data. Compare the hollow dream points with the real ones.
M7.Em.Plane.Tip: Point colour = responsibility-weighted mix of the component colours (soft assignment). Ellipses: 1σ and 2σ of each Gaussian; π: mixing weight. Hollow circles: dreamed samples.
M7.Em.Bayes.Tip: For the point under the mouse: prior π_k, likelihood N(u; μ_k, Σ_k) (scaled to the largest) and posterior p(k|u) of every component.
M7.Em.Likelihood.Tip: ⟨log p(u)⟩ after every EM iteration – it never decreases.
M7.Em.Probe.Hint: Move the mouse over the plane to see the posterior of a point.
M7.Sparse.Title: Sparse coding of natural images
M7.Sparse.Lead: PCA looks for global orthogonal directions that explain the most variance. Natural images, however, are better described locally: an edge, a contour or a texture element at a particular position and orientation. Sparse coding assumes that each input is explained by only a few active features out of many possible ones – and learns those features from the images.
M7.Sparse.C1.Title: Eigenfaces and the limits of PCA
M7.Sparse.C1.Text: Treating every image as a vector of N pixels, the eigenvectors of the image covariance can be drawn as images – for faces they are the “eigenfaces”. Keeping the first M components gives compression. But these eigenvectors are global patterns spanning the whole image (for patches: Fourier-like gratings); PCA does not enforce local parts such as an eye, a mouth or an edge. A different prior on the hidden coefficients is needed.
M7.Sparse.C2.Title: Linear generative model + sparse prior
M7.Sparse.C2.Text: u = G v + noise: the columns of the dictionary G are basis functions, v the hidden coefficients. Gaussian noise gives the likelihood exp(−½‖u − Gv‖²) – reconstruction error. The sparse prior says most v_i should be (nearly) zero and only a few strongly active: a distribution peaked at 0 with heavy tails (Laplace, Cauchy). Not all coefficients small – most of them silent.
M7.Sparse.C3.Title: MAP inference and learning the dictionary
M7.Sparse.C3.Text: Inference finds the most probable code: v* = argmin ½‖u − Gv‖² + λ‖v‖₁ – a compromise between good reconstruction and few active causes (the L1 term corresponds to a Laplace prior). Learning then adjusts G with τ_G dG/dt = (u − Gv)vᵀ: the product of the prediction error and the activity – a Hebbian-like rule that only learns what the model cannot yet explain.
M7.Sparse.C4.Title: What is learned: V1-like receptive fields
M7.Sparse.C4.Text: Trained on natural image patches, the dictionary columns become localized, oriented, band-pass edge and bar detectors – strikingly similar to the Gabor-like receptive fields of V1 simple cells (Olshausen & Field, 1996). This does not prove that cortex runs this algorithm, but it shows a strong normative link: natural image statistics plus efficient, sparse coding yield features that are found in biology.
M7.Sparse.Formulas:
u = Σ_i e_i v_i ≈ Σ_(i ≤ M) e_i v_i + noise | PCA / eigenfaces: global eigenvectors, compression by keeping M of them.
u = G v + noise,   p(u | v; G) ∝ exp(−½ ‖u − G v‖²) | Linear generative model and its Gaussian likelihood.
p(v) = Π_i p(v_i),   log p(v) = Σ_i log p(v_i) | Independent sparse prior (Laplace, Cauchy).
v* = argmin_v ½ ‖u − G v‖² + λ ‖v‖₁ | MAP inference: reconstruction error + sparsity penalty.
τ_G dG/dt = (u − G v) vᵀ | Dictionary learning: prediction error × activity.
M7.Sparse.Bio: Sparseness can mean population sparseness (few neurons respond strongly to a stimulus) or lifetime sparseness (a neuron responds strongly to few stimuli). Sparse codes save energy, separate features and have large capacity – but “the sparser the better” is not a universal law: the optimum depends on noise, metabolic cost and the task.
M7.Sparse.ML: The objective is LASSO / basis pursuit; learning G is dictionary learning, related to compressed sensing. With an overcomplete dictionary (more basis functions than pixels) the representation is not unique, and the sparse prior chooses the explanation with few components.
M7.Sparse.Takeaways:
PCA gives global components – good for compression, not for local parts.
Sparse coding: good reconstruction with few active hidden causes.
Objective: ½‖u − Gv‖² + λ‖v‖₁ (reconstruction error + sparsity penalty).
The dictionary learns with the error-driven, Hebbian-like rule ΔG ∝ (u − Gv)vᵀ.
On natural images it learns local, oriented, V1-like features.
M7.Sparse.Q1: Why is PCA not suitable for learning local image components?
M7.Sparse.A1: Its eigenvectors are typically global patterns, and orthogonality / variance maximization do not enforce locality.
M7.Sparse.Q2: What do G and v mean in the generative model u = Gv + noise?
M7.Sparse.A2: G is the learned dictionary (basis functions as columns), v the hidden coefficient or activity vector of the given input.
M7.Sparse.Q3: What is the typical objective of MAP sparse coding?
M7.Sparse.Q4: Why is the learning rule of G Hebbian-like?
M7.Sparse.A4: The update (u − Gv)vᵀ is the product of an error-like presynaptic signal and the latent (postsynaptic) activity.
M7.Sparse.Q5: What features does sparse coding learn from natural images, and why does it matter?
M7.Sparse.A5: Local, oriented edge and bar features that resemble the receptive fields of V1 simple cells – a link between image statistics, efficient coding and biology.
M7.Sparse.Guide:
Press “Learn” (or “Skip 250 steps”) and watch the 64 random basis functions turn into small oriented edges.
Tick “Compare with PCA”: the PCA components are global gratings, the sparse basis is local.
Click in the scene to choose a patch: only a few basis functions light up – the sparse code.
Raise λ: fewer causes are active, the reconstruction gets coarser.
Lower λ: the code gets dense and loses its edge-like character during learning.
M7.Sparse.SimpleTitle: In plain words: a box of stamps
M7.Sparse.Simple: Imagine you must redraw small pieces of photographs using a box of rubber stamps, but you may use only a handful of stamps per piece. A random set of stamps is useless. Each time you fail, you reshape the stamps a little towards what was missing. After many pieces the stamps become small lines and edges at all angles – because that is what natural pictures are made of. Remarkably, the cells of our primary visual cortex respond to exactly such small edges.
M7.Sparse.Learning.Tip: Each step: take 12 random patches, infer their sparse codes, then update G with η (u − Gv)vᵀ and renormalize the columns.
M7.Sparse.Lambda.Tip: Weight of the ‖v‖₁ penalty: larger λ → fewer active causes, coarser reconstruction.
M7.Sparse.FastForward.Tip: Runs 250 learning steps at once (about a second).
M7.Sparse.Scene.Tip: A synthetic natural-like image (occluding shapes with sharp edges at all orientations), whitened by a centre–surround filter like the retina. Click to choose the 8×8 patch to encode.
M7.Sparse.Dictionary.Tip: Every tile is one column of G drawn as an 8×8 image (grey = 0). Framed tiles are active in the code of the current patch; thicker frame = larger coefficient.
M7.Sparse.ComparePca.Tip: Shows the principal components of the same patches, ordered by explained variance.
M7.Sparse.Encode.Tip: Left: the patch u, its reconstruction Gv and the residual u − Gv. Right: the 64 coefficients v_k – most of them exactly zero.
M7.Sparse.CodeText: {0} of {1} causes active · {2}% of the patch explained
M7.Sparse.History.Tip: Relative reconstruction error and fraction of active coefficients per learning step.
M7.Predictive.Title: Predictive coding
M7.Predictive.Lead: In predictive coding the job of a representation is not just to pass the input on. Higher levels generate a prediction of the expected sensory activity; lower levels compute the difference between the actual input and the prediction, and mainly this prediction error is sent upwards. The brain does not merely receive its input – it keeps trying to explain it.
M7.Predictive.C1.Title: Prediction and prediction error
M7.Predictive.C1.Text: With the generative model of the previous lesson, the prediction is G v and the error u − G v. Inference changes v until the error becomes small while the representation stays as preferred by the prior. In this sense sparse coding is a special case of predictive coding: the internal representation tries at the same time to explain the input and to remain sparse.
M7.Predictive.C2.Title: The inference loop
M7.Predictive.C2.Text: Each iteration: feedback sends the prediction G v down; the lower level forms the error e = u − G v; the feedforward path sends Gᵀe up, which nudges the causes v; a threshold keeps most causes silent. Watch the energy fall: the reconstruction term decreases, the sparsity term grows as causes become active, and the total settles in a minimum.
M7.Predictive.C3.Title: Hierarchical predictive coding in the visual system
M7.Predictive.C3.Text: The visual cortex is strongly reciprocal: besides feedforward connections there are massive feedback projections. In the Rao–Ballard interpretation a higher area sends predictions of lower-level activity down, and the lower area sends the unexplained part – the error signal – up. The same principle can repeat at every level: retina/LGN → V1 → V2 → …
M7.Predictive.C4.Title: Not the same as backpropagation
M7.Predictive.C4.Text: Both use error-like signals, and under certain conditions links can be drawn between them, but their mechanism, goal and implementation differ. Predictive coding is primarily an inference framework: it adjusts the system's internal state so that its prediction fits the sensory data. Backpropagation computes parameter gradients of an explicit loss in supervised or self-supervised training.
M7.Predictive.Formulas:
prediction = G v,    prediction error = u − G v | What the higher level expects, and what it fails to explain.
τ_v dv/dt = Gᵀ(u − G v) − λ ∂‖v‖₁ | Inference: the fed-forward error updates the causes, the prior keeps them sparse.
E(v) = ½ ‖u − G v‖² + λ ‖v‖₁ | The energy that the loop minimizes.
τ_G dG/dt = (u − G v) vᵀ | Learning uses the same error signal.
M7.Predictive.Bio: Predictive coding offers explanations for extra-classical receptive-field effects (end-stopping), for mismatch and surprise responses (e.g. mismatch negativity in EEG), and for the abundance of feedback connections in cortex. Whether cortical layers really encode predictions and errors separately is an active research question.
M7.Predictive.ML: PCA/eigenfaces → low-rank representations; sparse coding → L1 regularization, LASSO, dictionary learning; u = Gv + noise → latent-variable and factor models; prediction-error learning → residual representations and error-driven updates. Hierarchical predictive coding is a biologically motivated relative of modern representation learning, but not the same as today's transformer or diffusion architectures.
M7.Predictive.Takeaways:
Predictive coding: feedback = prediction, feedforward = prediction error.
Inference iteratively changes the causes until the error is small and the code stays sparse.
Sparse coding is a special case of predictive coding.
Unexpected input leaves a large residual error – the signal of surprise.
Predictive coding is an inference framework, not the same as backpropagation.
M7.Predictive.Q1: What is the basic principle of predictive coding?
M7.Predictive.A1: The internal model sends predictions down, the lower level sends the prediction error up, and this refines the representation.
M7.Predictive.Q2: In what sense is sparse coding a special case of predictive coding?
M7.Predictive.A2: Its inference minimizes the prediction error u − Gv while keeping the code sparse – exactly a prediction–error loop with a sparse prior.
M7.Predictive.Q3: Why is predictive coding not the same as backpropagation?
M7.Predictive.A3: Predictive coding is primarily iterative inference in a generative prediction framework; backprop computes parameter gradients for an explicit loss.
M7.Predictive.Q4: What happens to the prediction error for an input the model cannot explain?
M7.Predictive.A4: It stays large: the learned causes cannot reproduce it – a surprise signal that would drive learning or attention.
M7.Predictive.Guide:
Press “Replay inference”: at iteration 0 everything is error; prediction grows, error shrinks.
Watch the hierarchy: the red (error) arrow thins as the blue (prediction) arrow thickens.
Choose “Edge”: a pattern the dictionary knows – explained almost completely by a few causes.
Choose “Noise”: the model cannot predict it, the error stays large – surprise.
Scrub the iteration slider to step through the loop.
M7.Predictive.SimpleTitle: In plain words: guess, check, correct
M7.Predictive.Simple: Your brain is not a camera. It constantly guesses what it is about to see and only pays real attention to what it got wrong. If you walk into your own kitchen, almost everything matches the guess and little news travels upwards. If there is an elephant in the kitchen, the guess fails badly – a large “error” signal rushes up and grabs your attention. In the lab, the blue arrow is the guess going down and the red arrow the surprise going up.
M7.Predictive.Untrained: The dictionary is still almost untrained, so predictions are poor. Train it in lesson 7.4 – or quickly here.
M7.Predictive.Stimulus.Tip: Natural: a patch of the scene. Edge: an oriented edge the dictionary can explain. Noise: white noise – unpredictable for the model.
M7.Predictive.Iteration.Tip: Step through the inference loop: at t = 0 nothing is predicted yet.
M7.Predictive.Hierarchy.Tip: Blue arrows: top-down predictions; red arrows: bottom-up prediction errors. Arrow width follows the size of the current signals.
M7.Predictive.Loop.Tip: Input u, current prediction G v(t) and the error u − G v(t) that is sent up; right: the causes v(t).

M7.Predictive.Explain.Surprise: Surprise: the learned causes can explain only {0}% of this input – a large prediction error remains and would be sent upwards.
